## CI for Difference of Means (Equal Variance)

::: {.callout title="Theorem 23.1"}
Let $X_{11}, X_{12}, \dots, X_{1n_1}$ be independent, normally distributed random variables with mean $\mu_1$ and unknown standard deviation $\sigma$ and let $X_{21}, X_{22}, \dots, X_{2n_2}$ be independent, normally distributed random variables with mean $\mu_2$ and unknown standard deviation $\sigma$, then an exact $100\times(1-\alpha)\%$ confidence interval for $\mu_1 - \mu_2$ is:

$$
\left((\bar{x}_1 - \bar{x}_2) - t_{n_1+n_2-2, 1-\alpha/2} \times s_p\sqrt{\frac{1}{n_1} + \frac{1}{n_2}}, (\bar{x}_1 - \bar{x}_2) + t_{n_1+n_2-2, 1-\alpha/2} \times s_p\sqrt{\frac{1}{n_1} + \frac{1}{n_2}}\right)
$$

where

$$
s_p = \sqrt{\frac{(n_1-1)s_1^2 + (n_2-1)s_2^2}{n_1 + n_2 - 2}}
$$

If the data are non-normal, but $n_1, n_2$ are sufficiently large, then this is an approximate $100 \times (1-\alpha)\%$ interval.
:::

A rule of thumb for determining equal variance is that $\max(s_1^2, s_2^2) \leq 4 \times \min(s_1^2, s_2^2)$

## CI for Difference of Means (Equal Variance, Proof Part 1)

The following has a standard normal distribution:

$$
\frac{(\bar{x}_1 - \bar{x}_2) -(\mu_1-\mu_2)}{\sigma\sqrt{\frac{1}{n_1} + \frac{1}{n_2}}} \sim N\left(0, 1\right)
$$

The following has a $\chi^2(n_1 + n_2 - 2)$ distribution:

$$
\frac{\sum_{i=1}^{n_1} (x_{i1} - \bar{x}_1)^2 + \sum_{i=1}^{n_2} (x_{i2} - \bar{x}_2)^2}{\sigma^2} \sim \chi^2(n_1 + n_2 - 2)
$$

## CI for Difference of Means (Equal Variance, Proof Part 2)

The following is a standard normal random variable divided by the square root of an independent $\chi^2_{n_1+n_2-2}$ random variable divided by its degrees of freedom. By definition this is a $t_{n_1+n_2-2}$ random variable:

$$
\frac{\frac{(\bar{x}_1 - \bar{x}_2) -(\mu_1-\mu_2)}{\sigma\sqrt{\frac{1}{n_1} + \frac{1}{n_2}}}}{\sqrt{\frac{\sum_{i=1}^{n_1} (x_{i1} - \bar{x}_1)^2 + \sum_{i=1}^{n_2} (x_{i2} - \bar{x}_2)^2}{(n_1+n_2-2)\sigma^2}}} \sim t(n_1+n_2-2)
$$

Simplifying this results in the following:

$$
\frac{(\bar{x}_1 - \bar{x}_2) -(\mu_1-\mu_2)}{\sqrt{\frac{(n_1-1)s_1^2 + (n_2-1)s_2^2}{n_1 + n_2 - 2}\left(\frac{1}{n_1} + \frac{1}{n_2}\right)}} \sim t(n_1 + n_2 - 2)
$$

## Ex: Drug Study (1)

::: {.callout title="Example 23.1"}
You are comparing two drugs to see how effective they are in reducing blood pressure. First, you get a baseline blood pressure measurement for everyone in the study. You then randomly assign 35 patients to receive drug A and 35 patients to receive drug B. After two weeks, you record the reduction in blood pressure from the baseline and find that $\bar{x}_A = -5$, $\bar{x}_B = -3$, $s_A^2 = 10$, and $s_B^2 = 14$.

Compute the standard error needed to construct a 95% confidence interval for $\mu_A - \mu_B$.
:::

. . .

```{r, echo = TRUE}
s2_A <- 10
s2_B <- 14
n_A <- 35
n_B <- 35
max(s2_A, s2_B) <= 4*min(s2_A, s2_B)

sp <- sqrt(((n_A-1)*s2_A + (n_B-1)*s2_B)/(n_A+n_B-2))
se <- sp*sqrt(1/n_A + 1/n_B)
se
```

## Ex: Drug Study (2)

::: {.callout title="Example 23.2"}
You are comparing two drugs to see how effective they are in reducing blood pressure. First, you get a baseline blood pressure measurement for everyone in the study. You then randomly assign 35 patients to receive drug A and 35 patients to receive drug B. After two weeks, you record the reduction in blood pressure from the baseline and find that $\bar{x}_A = -5$, $\bar{x}_B = -3$, $s_A^2 = 10$, and $s_B^2 = 14$.

Construct a 95% confidence interval for $\mu_A - \mu_B$.
:::

. . .

```{r, echo = TRUE}
xbar_A <- -5
xbar_B <- -3
alpha <- 0.05
t_quant <- qt(1-alpha/2, n_A+n_B-2)

(xbar_A-xbar_B) + c(-1,1)*t_quant*se
```

## Ex: Fuel

::: {.callout title="Example 23.7"}
You are investigating two different types of additives for engine oil lubricants, call them Additive A and Additive B. You would like to see if Additive A results in higher fuel efficiency than Additive B. Scientists have 40 tests with Additive A and 45 tests with Additive B and recorded the fuel efficiency (in mpg) for each test, which can be found below:

```{r, echo = TRUE}
fuel_A <- c(32, 31, 29.7, 28.3, 30.3, 27.3, 31.4, 28.8, 28.9, 30.9, 30, 31,
            34.8, 31.1, 32.7, 29.4, 27.8, 33.3, 27.8, 22, 31.9, 37.1, 26,
            30.9, 28.8, 35, 32.1, 28.9, 24, 26, 33.6, 32.7, 35.4, 34, 34.7,
            27.7, 26.9, 29.7, 25.8, 33.8)

fuel_B <- c(26.2, 27.7, 26.2, 26.2, 25.1, 24.2, 29.3, 23.4, 24.5, 25.9,
            31.3, 25.1, 29, 25.5, 27.8, 25.5, 30.2, 28.2, 28.8, 25.1,
            24.3, 26.6, 28.2, 29.7, 33.6, 30.1, 24.5, 25.8, 25.9, 31,
            27.7, 31, 30.7, 31.1, 21.8, 21.6, 25.6, 23.1, 30.5, 27.6,
            25.2, 32.4, 31.9, 30.3, 29.6)
```

You would like to construct a 95% confidence interval for $\mu_A - \mu_B$.
:::

## Ex: Fuel, Continued

```{r, echo = TRUE}
xbar_A <- mean(fuel_A); xbar_B <- mean(fuel_B)
s2_A <- var(fuel_A); s2_B <- var(fuel_B)
max(s2_A, s2_B) <= 4*min(s2_A, s2_B)
n_A <- length(fuel_A); n_B <- length(fuel_B)
alpha <- 0.05
t_quant <- qt(1-alpha/2, n_A + n_B - 2)
sp <- sqrt(((n_A-1)*s2_A + (n_B-1)*s2_B)/(n_A+n_B-2))
se <- sp*sqrt(1/n_A + 1/n_B)

(xbar_A - xbar_B) + c(-1, 1)*t_quant*se
```

```{r, echo = TRUE}
t.test(fuel_A, fuel_B, var.equal = TRUE, conf.level = 0.95)$conf.int[1:2]
```

            200.5, 199.9, 200.1, 201.3, 200.5, 199.8, 200.2, 200.3, 200.1, 199.7, 201.0, 200.4, 200.2, 199.9,

## CI for Difference of Means (Unequal Variance)

::: {.callout title="Theorem 23.2"}
Let $X_{11}, X_{12}, \dots, X_{1n_1}$ be independent random variables with mean $\mu_1$ and unknown standard deviation $\sigma_1$ and let $X_{21}, X_{22}, \dots, X_{2n_2}$ be independent random variables with mean $\mu_2$ and unknown standard deviation $\sigma_2$ where $\sigma_1, \neq \sigma_2$ and assume $n_1, n_2$ are sufficiently large. Then an approximate $100\times(1-\alpha)\%$ confidence interval for $\mu_1 - \mu_2$ is:

$$
\left((\bar{x}_1 - \bar{x}_2) - t_{df, 1-\alpha/2} \times \sqrt{\frac{s_1^2}{n_1} + \frac{s_2^2}{n_2}}, (\bar{x}_1 - \bar{x}_2) + t_{df, 1-\alpha/2} \times \sqrt{\frac{s_1^2}{n_1} + \frac{s_2^2}{n_2}}\right)
$$

where

$$
df = \frac{\left(\frac{s_1^2}{n_1} + \frac{s_2^2}{n_2}\right)^2}{\frac{s_1^4/n_1^2}{n_1-1} + \frac{s_2^4/n_2^2}{n_2-1}}
$$
:::

A rule of thumb for determining whether variances are equal is that $\max(s_1^2, s_2^2) \leq 4 \times \min(s_1^2, s_2^2)$

## Ex: Paper Towels

::: {.callout title="Example 23.10"}
You are testing two different brands of paper towels (brand A and brand B) to see which can is more absorbent. You take a random sample of 40 squares of paper towels from brand A and 40 squares of paper towels from brand B. You then measure how much water in grams the towel can absorb before breaking. You record the following statistics $\bar{x}_A = 59, \bar{x}_B = 64, s_A^2 = 6, s_B^2 = 35$. Construct a 95% confidence interval for $\mu_A - \mu_B$.
:::

. . .

```{r, echo = TRUE}
n_A <- 40
n_B <- 40
xbar_A <- 59
xbar_B <- 64
s2_A <- 6
s2_B <- 35
alpha <- 0.05

max(s2_A, s2_B) <= 4*min(s2_A, s2_B)
df <- (s2_A/n_A + s2_B/n_B)^2/(s2_A^2/(n_A^2*(n_A-1)) + s2_B^2/(n_B^2*(n_B-1)))
t_quant <- qt(1-alpha/2, df)

(xbar_A - xbar_B) + c(-1, 1)*t_quant*sqrt(s2_A/n_A + s2_B/n_B)
```

## Ex: Gaming

::: {.callout title="Example 23.11"}
You are testing two different gaming controllers (brand A and brand B) to determine which has a faster response time. You take a random sample of 30 players using brand A and 35 players using brand B. You then measure their average response times in milliseconds when pressing a button in a standardized test. The results are: $\bar{x}_A = 152, \bar{x}_B = 145, s_A^2 = 70, s_B^2 = 15$. Construct a 90% confidence interval for $\mu_A - \mu_B$.
:::

. . .

```{r, echo = TRUE}
n_A <- 30 
n_B <- 35
xbar_A <- 152
xbar_B <- 145
s2_A <- 70
s2_B <- 15
alpha <- 0.1

max(s2_A, s2_B) <= 4*min(s2_A, s2_B)
df <- (s2_A/n_A + s2_B/n_B)^2/(s2_A^2/(n_A^2*(n_A-1)) + s2_B^2/(n_B^2*(n_B-1)))
t_quant <- qt(1-alpha/2, df)

(xbar_A - xbar_B) + c(-1, 1)*t_quant*sqrt(s2_A/n_A + s2_B/n_B)
```

## Ex: Incomes

::: {.callout title="Example 23.13"}
You are interested in comparing annual incomes for software engineers (in thousands) in two different cities, city A and city B. You collect a random sample of 35 salaries from city A and 40 salaries from city B. Use the data below to construct a 95% confidence interval for $\mu_A - \mu_B$.

```{r, echo = TRUE}
city_A <- c(80, 85, 79, 76, 74, 70, 91, 80, 77, 79, 74, 85, 84, 81, 87, 77, 79, 84, 88, 88, 
            84, 74, 73, 80, 74, 77, 70, 69, 83, 81, 79, 89, 69, 73, 88)

city_B <- c(121, 39, 44, 90, 70, 101, 63, 121, 111, 104, 81, 92, 90, 108, 92, 86, 98, 128, 
            98, 99, 37, 52, 92, 86, 94, 84, 111, 43, 51, 58, 122, 174, 76, 82, 116, 106, 53, 16, 18, 7)
```
:::

. . .

```{r, echo = TRUE}
max(var(city_A), var(city_B)) <= 4*min(var(city_A), var(city_B))

xbar_A <- mean(city_A); xbar_B <- mean(city_B)
s2_A <- var(city_A); s2_B <- var(city_B)
n_A <- length(city_A); n_B <- length(city_B)
alpha <- 0.05

df <- (s2_A/n_A + s2_B/n_B)^2/(s2_A^2/(n_A^2*(n_A-1)) + s2_B^2/(n_B^2*(n_B-1)))
t_quant <- qt(1-alpha/2, df)
(xbar_A - xbar_B) + c(-1, 1)*t_quant*sqrt(s2_A/n_A + s2_B/n_B)
```
